solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Scottish hero gives Hibernian pro licence

indicators.note: gives in the sense of yields or buckles, so the letters of the following words bend into a new order

explanation.surface: A Scottish champion grants a licence to a professional footballer from Hibernian, the Edinburgh club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives' signals that HIBERNIANPROLICENCE, all nineteen letters, is rearranged. Hibernian is an Edinburgh football club, which makes 'Scottish hero' sound like a sporting star.
explanation.definitionFit: The Young Pretender, Charles Edward Stuart, who led the 1745 Jacobite rising, is a celebrated figure of Scottish legend.

clue.text: Braggart with bit of straw in hat

indicators.note: in places the small piece inside the headgear named next

parts.note: a boater is a flat-topped straw hat

indicators.note: a bit of the word straw is just its opening letter

explanation.surface: A show-off sports a straw hat with a wisp poking out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bit of' takes the S of straw, which 'in' puts inside BOATER, a stiff straw hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A braggart is someone who brags, a direct synonym for one who talks himself up.

clue.text: Complete turn around in New York to cancel out

indicators.note: in places the reversed letters between the two letters for the city
around signals the preceding pair of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: to complete, as a form, is to fill it
U as in a U-turn

explanation.surface: Someone makes a complete about-turn in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' turns FILL + U into ULLIF, and 'in' puts that between N and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: To nullify is to make void or negate, the same as cancelling out an effect.

clue.text: Wild eglantine not the herb of grace?

indicators.note: wild suggests something unruly, telling us to rearrange the flower's name

explanation.surface: A rambling sweet-briar is wondered not to be the plant traditionally called herb of grace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' rearranges EGLANTINE, the sweet-briar rose. The herb of grace is rue, which makes the definition look botanical, but it really means 'lacking grace', with 'the herb' pointing back at eglantine.
explanation.definitionFit: Inelegant means lacking grace or polish, so a plant wildly rearranged into it is one without grace.

clue.text: Fathom more than fruit

definitions.meaning: to fathom is to sound the depth of, as with a weighted line
the word is a fruit name with one letter more, a playful second reading

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a joke: the answer is the fruit PLUM and then something more (a B).
explanation.definitionFit: To plumb the depths is to fathom them, both meaning measure or understand fully.

clue.text: Understanding in view

parts.note: something in view is in sight

explanation.walkthrough: 'in view' reads as a single phrase meaning visible; split into two words it supplies the whole answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Insight is a deep understanding of a person or situation, a near synonym.

clue.text: Odd dog takes notes

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog
IOUs are written promissory notes, so plural notes give IOUS

explanation.surface: A strange hound is seen jotting things down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takes' is a link here joining CUR to IOUS; 'notes' are IOUs, signed promises to pay.
explanation.definitionFit: Curious can mean strange or unusual, the same sense as odd.

clue.text: Drink at silly cost which effects heaven

indicators.note: silly suggests muddled, so the letters of the two words are scrambled

parts.note: the sky is the heavens

explanation.surface: A drink at a ridiculous price that brings on bliss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly' rearranges the letters of 'cost which', and the heaven synonym follows; 'effects' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Malt or blended spirit distilled in Scotland is a familiar drink ordered in any bar.

clue.text: See 1
Ban Ki-Moon's employees relax

parts.note: Ban Ki-Moon was Secretary-General of the UN, so his organisation is the UN's
a crew is a group of workers

explanation.surface: Staff of a former UN Secretary-General take it easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ban' looks like a verb but is part of a name: Ban Ki-Moon headed the United Nations.
explanation.definitionFit: To unscrew a fitting is to loosen or slacken it, as relax can mean loosen.

clue.text: I leave attendants and appear among experts with fowler

indicators.note: the letter I departs from the first word named
the departed letter then shows up inside the second word named

parts.note: waiters attend on diners
a panel is a group of experts

explanation.surface: A guest drops the staff and joins the expert judges, accompanied by a bird shooter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I leave' turns WAITERS into WATERS, and 'appear among' puts that I into PANEL, giving PANIEL.
explanation.definitionFit: This gundog breed retrieves shot waterfowl, so it is the dog that goes out alongside a wildfowler.

clue.text: Boy seizing model — diamonds are for the birds

indicators.note: seizing means the boy's name grips the next piece inside it

parts.note: Tim is a boy's name
the Model T was Ford's famous car
ice is slang for diamonds

explanation.surface: A lad grabs a model, but diamonds, it seems, are worthless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are for the birds' is an idiom for 'worthless', which hides the definition 'the birds'; 'seizing' puts T inside TIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Small songbirds such as blue tits are known collectively by this old plural.

clue.text: More than 12 inches of cryptozoology?

parts.note: a twelve-inch measure is a foot, and this one from the study of legendary beasts is outsized

explanation.walkthrough: Twelve inches make a foot; cryptozoology studies unproven creatures such as the North American hairy giant known by its huge tracks.
explanation.definitionFit: The ape-like creature of North American legend is named for its enormous footprints.

clue.text: Boy that won't leave alone?

definitions.meaning: to harass someone persistently is not to leave them alone

explanation.definitionFit: To harry is to pester or harass, and it is also a common male first name.

clue.text: Antipasto is a f-favourite first with the Queen

indicators.note: first places the stammered favourite ahead of the word is

parts.note: pet means favourite, and the stammer repeats the opening letter
ER, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Someone stammers that a starter is their f-favourite, served first to the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter in 'f-favourite' is copied onto the synonym, doubling its opening letter. 'first' puts that before 'is'; the Queen is Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian antipasto is a starter, a small dish served before the main meal.

clue.text: Religious student abandons gambling game for a bit of dancing

parts.note: pi is informal for pious or religious

indicators.note: abandons means the learner's letter is dropped from the game

parts.note: roulette is the casino wheel game
L, a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A devout learner gives up the casino wheel in favour of a little dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abandons' drops the learner's letter from the casino game; L-plates mark British learner drivers.
explanation.definitionFit: A pirouette is a spin on one foot, a single movement within a dance.

clue.text: Limit of flood that comes with hell

definitions.meaning: the highest level reached by a tide or flood
from the phrase come hell or ... meaning whatever happens

explanation.definitionFit: High water is the peak level of a tide or flood, and the idiom pairs it with hell.

clue.text: Better not climb a eucalyptus?

parts.note: being up such an Australian tree is an idiom for being in trouble, so climbing one is unwise

explanation.walkthrough: 'Up a gum tree' is a British idiom for being stuck in a difficult position.
explanation.definitionFit: Eucalyptus trees are popularly called by this name for the resin they exude.

clue.text: Scottish hero a winner with every one

parts.note: all means every one
an ace in tennis is a winning serve

explanation.surface: A Scottish champion who triumphs with everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: William Wallace led the Scots against Edward I in the 1290s. The pieces are written in answer order: W, ALL, ACE.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wallace, the medieval freedom fighter, is a national figure revered in Scotland.

clue.text: Auntie's lost some energy with work on jazz

indicators.note: lost some means one of the energy letters is dropped

parts.note: Auntie and the Beeb are both nicknames for the BBC
E is the symbol for energy
OP, short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: The BBC loses some of its energy, working on jazz programmes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost some' drops one of the two energy letters from the nickname, and 'on' puts work after it. Auntie is a fond British nickname for the BBC.
explanation.definitionFit: Bebop is a fast, complex style of jazz developed in the 1940s.

clue.text: Flirting with eyelids at the crease

definitions.meaning: the crease is where the batter stands in cricket, so in the middle of an innings

explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the batter stands at the crease, a line marked in front of the stumps.
explanation.definitionFit: One flutters or bats eyelids to flirt, and in cricket a player on strike is in the process of batting.

clue.text: Nothing extraterrestrial is warmer

parts.note: a blank is an empty space, nothing
ET, the film alien

explanation.surface: Nothing from outer space is hotter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'warmer' looks like a comparative adjective but is a noun: something that keeps you warm.
explanation.definitionFit: A bed covering keeps a sleeper warm, so it is a warmer in the noun sense.

clue.text: One having a taste for embroidery

definitions.meaning: someone who tries a bit of food or drink
a piece of needlework displaying various stitches

explanation.definitionFit: A taster tries samples, and a traditional embroidered panel shows a range of stitches.

clue.text: Job specification — watch back!

indicators.note: back says the device for keeping time is read in reverse

parts.note: a timer, like a watch, measures time

explanation.surface: A demand on a job description: look behind you!
explanation.walkthrough: 'watch back!' looks like a warning, but 'back' reverses TIMER.
explanation.definitionFit: A remit is the defined scope of responsibility given to someone, as a job specification sets out.

clue.text: Puritan's arranged transport for London

indicators.note: arranged suggests sorting into a new order

parts.note: the possessive s gives no letter

explanation.surface: A puritan has organised travel to the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arranged' rearranges PURITAN. On British railways a train heading towards London is going 'up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trains travelling towards the capital are known on British railways as up trains, carrying people towards London.

clue.text: Feet and other body part going on mast

parts.note: a yard is three feet
the arm is another body part, after the feet

explanation.surface: Feet and arm both go on board the mast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Feet' means a measure, three feet making a yard, not a body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The yardarm is the end of a spar fixed across a ship's mast to hang sail.

clue.text: It doesn't charge much — down with economic theory!

definitions.meaning: a slow, low-current charge for batteries
the theory that wealth at the top filters down to the poor

explanation.definitionFit: A slow charge keeps a battery topped up, and the economic theory supposes benefits seep down.

clue.text: Occurrence with old solvers in view — is this a record?

indicators.note: in tells us the pieces go inside the word for view

parts.note: sight means view
an event is an occurrence
ye is the old word for you, the solvers

explanation.surface: An event involving veteran puzzlers comes into view: might this be a record?
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' splits the view word after its first letter to take the two pieces. Old gramophone records spun at this many revolutions a minute.
explanation.definitionFit: Shellac discs that played at seventy-eight rpm were called by that number.
